name: Al-Uqlidisi board reckoning
summary: Calculation on a dust board, where digits were rubbed out and shifted as the work went on, as described by al-Uqlidisi in Damascus.
description: The erasable-board arithmetic taken as the starting configuration in al-Uqlidisi's treatment: digits and intermediate results can be erased or shifted during calculation.
tier_reason: Board reckoning can be fine detail, but it is the contrasting method in an adaptation and therefore is not a duplicate of paper reckoning. This is a scoped consequence judgement, not a reward for documentation or representation.

date.label: By 952–953
date.basis: Al-Uqlīdisī’s text was composed in 952–953 and describes a contemporary social use.

events.statement: Al-Uqlīdisī associates the dust board with people earning a living by astrology in the streets.
events.place_note: Medieval Islamic world; no single location
events.caveats: The account survives through a later copy; the source does not establish that all such astrologers were in Damascus or that all used identical boards.

evidence.locator: Section 1.3, paragraphs on dust board and al-Uqlīdisī’s innovations
evidence.supports: Relates erasable-board calculation to a professional group and dates the text.

evidence.locator: Chapter 1 PDF pp. 14–15, description of al-Uqlīdisī and textual survival
evidence.supports: Provides the later manuscript transmission context.

date.basis: Composition of Chapters on Indian Arithmetic in Damascus, dated 341 AH; this is a textual attestation, not the invention of board calculation.

events.statement: The erasable-board arithmetic taken as the starting configuration in al-Uqlidisi's treatment: digits and intermediate results can be erased or shifted during calculation.
events.caveats: No preserved tenth-century board is claimed. This node dates the described practice in the book, not its first regional use.

evidence.supports: Dates the composition and distinguishes the earlier arithmetic treatment from Book IV's paper methods.

evidence.locator: Printed pp. 173–175, especially Book IV discussion on p. 174
evidence.supports: Explicitly contrasts ink-and-paper methods with the dust board used before.
